title: Don't crowd them
hook: don't cramp people's homes or weary their lives (Tao Te Ching 72)

segments.voice: Yesterday, knowing you don't know. Your line was I don't know. Did you get to say it, and what came after? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

A teenager's bedroom door, closed. On the other side of it, a parent with a question, a reminder, and a worry, all lined up. Knock now, and the door may stay closed for a week. Wait an hour, and it might open on its own. Either side of that door is a hard place to stand. Chapter seventy-two of the Tao Te Ching is written to rulers, but it's about that hallway.
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR.` → `A QUESTION LINED UP.` → `KNOCK, OR WAIT?`

segments.voice: First, the warning. The chapter opens: when people no longer fear what's fearsome, something far more fearsome arrives. Pile on enough pressure and the pressure stops working, and what comes next is worse. Second, the instruction. Don't cramp the places where people live. Don't weary the lives they lead. The old words are physical: don't press in on their dwellings, don't make them sick of living. And then a neat loop: only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you. Third, the sage's own room. The sage, the chapter says, knows himself but doesn't put himself on show, and cares for himself but doesn't set himself up high. There's a link here. Someone who doesn't need to be seen, or to be above, has less reason to crowd anyone else. Fourth, the week. It ends here, so look back. Rivers and seas lead because they lie lower. Three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward. Coarse cloth with jade inside. Knowing you don't know. Today's chapter fits the run: they're all ways of taking up less space so that others have more. On an ordinary Tuesday, room looks like a question asked once instead of three times. A plan left open for someone else to fill. Not reading over a shoulder.
screen: `PRESSURE STOPS WORKING.` · `DON'T CRAMP THEIR HOMES.` · `NO NEED TO BE SEEN.` · `A WEEK OF TAKING LESS SPACE.` · then, large: `GIVE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone room. Sit and let your breath find its own pace; don't push it, just give it room too. Then bring to mind one person you've been pressing on, even gently. A child, a partner, a coworker, a friend who owes you a reply. Picture the space around them, and leave it empty for a moment. What would you stop asking, checking, or reminding, just for today? Choose one thing. Rest with the space that leaves. The bell holds the time.
Don't crowd them. Chapter seventy-two: don't cramp where people live or weary the lives they lead; if you don't weary them, they won't weary of you. Today's word.
Your line: give room. Today, ask once, then wait. Let one person come to you in their own time. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-two as advice on governing and on any kind of authority: don't press in on people's homes or lives, and they won't turn against you.

it's a loop: give room, and you're given room back.

fork.setup: you have authority over others and they've grown tired of you. what does chapter seventy-two advise?
options: press harder so they fear you again.
stop cramping their homes and wearying their lives.
fork.reveal: the chapter says don't cramp where they live or weary their lives. only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you.

original.note: Chinese: don't press in on where they live, from chapter seventy-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't crowd them is about personal space.
what it means: pressure past a point backfires; leaving people room to live is what keeps the peace.
what a scholar hears: the chapter plays on one word for 'weary' twice, so not wearying others and not being wearied are the same move.

notes: Week-end day: looks back at days 1128–1133; the editor checked the recap against those scripts.
The three treasures are named here as gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first, matching day 1129's Legge wording (chapter 67).
Chapter 72 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording. The opening line 民不畏威，則大威至 is read here as a warning about pressure backfiring; some read 威 differently. Confirm.
Trapdoor: 厭 (yàn) is used twice in 夫唯不厭，是以不厭; confirm.
Original 無狎其所居 (wú xiá qí suǒ jū) rendered 'woo SHYAH chee swaw JYOO'. Some editions read 狹 for 狎. Confirm.
Editor: the three treasures now use day 1129's wording (gentleness, economy) instead of kindness, frugality; the practice no longer repeats day 1131's stepping-back image.
